sentences.text: Masiakasaurus knopfleri is the sole species within its extinct genus, representing a small predatory theropod that measured between 1.8 and 2 meters in length.
This dinosaur possessed a unique set of front teeth that projected forward, with the leading tooth angled just ten degrees above the horizontal plane.
Unlike many theropods with curved necks, Masiakasaurus had a stiff neck supported by thick ribs and held almost horizontally with only a slight bend.
It also retained longer forelimbs compared to the extremely reduced arms seen in other abelisaurids.
Recent research from 2026 indicates this animal may have possessed adaptations for catching small prey, echoing roles played by larger tyrannosaurs and abelisaurids.
The genus was officially named in the year 2001 by paleontologists Scott D. Sampson, Matthew Carrano, and Catherine A. Forster.
Fossil remains were first described in the journal Nature that same year, originating from Late Cretaceous deposits located in northwestern Madagascar.
Further specimens belonging to this genus were subsequently described in 2011.
The unusual arrangement of its teeth points to a specialized diet, potentially including fish, small vertebrates, invertebrates, and perhaps even fruit.
Scientists have noted the existence of both robust and gracile body forms, which might indicate sexual dimorphism or represent two separate populations.
Reaching the size of a large dog took eight to ten years, a growth rate forty percent slower than similar non-avian theropods but forty percent faster than crocodylians.
A right scapulocoracoid bone shows holes that could be puncture marks from predators, possibly including the large abelisaurid Majungasaurus.
Conversely, the large snake Madtsoia madagascariensis might have attempted to eat an adult Masiakasaurus, though such a large meal would likely have been injurious for the snake.
Masiakasaurus belonged to the family Noasauridae, a group of small predatory ceratosaurs primarily found in South America and other parts of Gondwana.
In 2002, Carrano and colleagues formally placed the genus in Noasauridae alongside Laevisuchus and Noasaurus.
This animal lived during the Late Cretaceous period, specifically within the Maastrichtian age.
Approximately seventy million years ago, it shared its environment with creatures such as Majungasaurus, Rapetosaurus, and Rahonavis.
